Towards Generalizable Image Classification  Models for Detecting Middle Ear Diseases
Manfred Lindmark1, Thorbjörn Lundberg2, Mimmi Werner3, Paolo Soda4, 1, Christer  Grönlund1, Fredrik Öhberg1
1Department of Diagnostics and Intervention, Biomedical Engineering and Radiation Physics, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden   2Department of Public Health and Clinical Medicine, Unit of Family Medicine, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden   3Department of Clinical Sciences, Otorhinolaryngology, Umeå University, Umeå, Sweden  4Research Unit of Computer Systems and Bioinformatics, Department of Engineering, Università Campus Bio-Medico di Roma, Rome, Italy
Corresponding author: Manfred Lindmark (e-mail: manfred.lindmark@umu.se).
This work was funded by Centrala ALF ref. RV-979824, the University Hospital of Umeå, the Swedish Research Council and Sweden's  innovation agency VINNOVA.
ABSTRACT Diagnosing ear diseases from images of the tympanic membrane has emerged as a promising  application for deep learning-based classification models. While several studies report high diagnostic  accuracy, these models often struggle to generalize to external data that does not match the image  characteristics of the training data. This study aims to evaluate methods for enhancing model generalizability.  We trained artificial neural networks on tympanic membrane images from five datasets with a large  heterogeneity between them. The datasets consisted of images from different countries, captured with  different otoscope models, and with different image pre-processing applied at the source (e.g., colour  normalization, cropping, and resolution). Artificial neural networks for binary (normal/abnormal)  classification were trained on three datasets, and the models were evaluated on two. We explored several  strategies to improve generalizability, including image pre-processing, data augmentation, transfer learning,  and different network architectures. The effects of each investigated factor and their interactions were  determined through a full factorial experimental design and linear mixed-effects model. Our best  classification network achieved a mean accuracy of 83% (sensitivity 71%, specificity 91%) on external  datasets. In contrast, the baseline trained without an optimized training method and using non-processed  datasets yielded an accuracy of 53% (sensitivity 83%, specificity 34%). Our findings highlight how a better  choice of network, training and augmentation strategies, and data verification improve model generalizability.
INDEX TERMS Artificial intelligence, diagnostic imaging, generalizability, medical image classification,  otitis media.
I. INTRODUCTION  Globally, one in five people live with hearing loss, and  most of them lack access to interventions [1]. Many of these  cases are preventable with early detection and treatment. In  pediatric care, a very common diagnosis is acute otitis  media (AOM), which may need antibiotic treatment to  avoid severe complications. In underserved areas, where  there are few specialists available to diagnose ear diseases,  there is a need for new diagnostic tools that do not require  specialist knowledge or expensive equipment. This is one  of the motivations for developing computer vision-based  diagnostic support systems.  Computer vision models can be used for the classification  of ear diseases from images of the tympanic membrane
(TM; Figure 1) taken by simple digital otoscopes. In the last  years several studies have shown that using deep learning  (DL) methods such as convolutional neural networks  (CNNs) for the identification of different ear diseases can  outperform general practitioners when using only an image  of the ear drum as input [2]. However, there are several

challenges left before these systems are practical for  clinical use.   A first challenge is the reproducibility of earlier DL  methods, which is often constrained by inadequate  documentation of model implementation and training  hyperparameters, or the use of proprietary datasets [3].  Another issue is the generalizability of machine learning  (ML) models. Model accuracies can be very high on test  sets derived from the training data, but when the model  encounters  new  input  that  does  not  match  the  characteristics of the training data, accuracy often drops  considerably [4]. This phenomenon is known as dataset or  domain shift and has many possible causes [5]. Domain  shift is a well-known issue in medical image classification,  and presents in the form of either covariate shift caused by  changes in image characteristics, or concept shift caused by  inter-rater variability [6]. It is not reasonable to be able to  anticipate and compensate for all possible future shifts in  the data distribution when the domain is as complex and  high-dimensional as medical images. In practice it is more  common to manually monitor a deployed ML system to  identify changes in the input or decreasing model accuracy  to update the model when needed, but ideally the system  should be as robust as possible to these changes [4]. Despite  that, in the recent literature, we have observed the rise of
foundation models, which have shown promise in  addressing the challenges posed by shifts in data  distribution, particularly in complex, high-dimensional  domains like medical imaging [7]. These models are trained  on extensive and diverse datasets, enabling them to learn  generalizable representations that can capture variations  across a wide range of input scenarios. This foundational  knowledge can allow them to handle new, unseen data  distributions more effectively than traditional models,  thereby reducing the frequency and extent of manual  intervention needed post-deployment.  DL methods using large neural networks typically perform  better when it comes to generalization as compared to  traditional ML, but because of their high capacity, they also  tend to over-fit to less general characteristics or biases of  the training data. Training a deep neural network (DNN) to  generalize well and achieve good accuracy requires a large  amount of data that captures as much variability in the  domain as possible [8].  In medical applications, data scarcity becomes a problem  because acquiring new data is costly, and data sharing is  subject to privacy concerns and ethics review approval. In  the case of tympanic membrane images taken by digital  otoscope/endoscope, there are currently only three publicly  available datasets published, each covering a different set  of ear conditions [9], [10], [11]. A recent study showed that  when training an image classifier on one of these three  datasets and then evaluating its performance on one of the  others, the accuracy was severely reduced [12]. This result  agrees with previous considerations, and it can be  understood intuitively by looking at the visual difference  between the samples in the datasets given the use of  different otoscopes, subject demographics, and image  preprocessing techniques employed. It was then shown that  training a model on all three datasets will improve accuracy  on a test set from any of the individual datasets, which is  expected when the training and test data are from similar  distributions [12]. Although this shows the benefit of  having as much varied data as possible, a limitation is that  it does not tell us how good the model will perform on  future data with another unknown dataset shift.  Recent work has also examined biases within these specific  datasets. Xu et al. [13] systematically analyzed the same  three public datasets used here for training (Türkiye, Chile,  and Ohio/USA) and showed, through counterfactual  masking and color-feature experiments, that classifiers can  achieve high internal performance by exploiting non- clinical artifacts (illumination, color saturation, image  framing, and near-duplicate images) rather than clinically  meaningful features. This shows the importance of both the  data-quality review and the strict external-dataset  evaluation used in this study.  Cross-dataset generalization and benchmarking have  received growing attention in the medical image  classification literature. Matta et al. [6] reviewed

generalization research in medical imaging, identifying  domain shift as a pervasive challenge across modalities and  underlining the importance of multi-source evaluation. The  present study builds on this by applying a structured  experimental design to quantify the relative importance of  several generalization-improving strategies in the otoscopy  domain.  The aim of this study was to investigate different methods  to improve model generalizability (without having more  data) when using a DNN-based image classifier for  detecting abnormal tympanic membranes. For this task we  added two additional TM image repositories [14], [15], [16]  in addition to the three above-mentioned datasets for a  wider representation of domain shifts. To pursue this goal,  we identified three sub-aims. The first was to show the  problem of using a single source of data, and the difference  an improved model training approach can make. The  second aim was to compare the importance of which neural  network architecture is used in relation to the different  generalizability-improving methods applied when training  the network. The final aim was to quantify the effects and  interactions of several different generalizability-improving  methods through statistical methods, to understand which  are the most effective and if there are synergistic effects.  For the second and third aim we used the first three datasets  to train the model and used the last two as an external test  set with a considerable domain shift.  The main contributions of this study are: (1) a systematic  empirical  evaluation  of  multiple  generalizability- improving methods across five heterogeneous tympanic  membrane image datasets with substantial domain shift; (2)  a full factorial experimental design enabling statistical  quantification of the main effects and interaction effects of  network architecture, training method, augmentation  strategy, and data quality on cross-dataset performance;  and (3) a publicly available implementation of the  optimized training pipeline to facilitate reproducibility.  While the individual methods are not novel in isolation,  their systematic comparison in a cross-dataset medical  imaging context, and the resulting guidance on which  factors matter most, constitutes the primary contribution of  this work.
II. METHODS  A. GENERALIZABILITY-IMPROVING METHODS IN DEEP  LEARNING  1) TRANSFER LEARNING  Transfer learning refers to using a model trained on a  separate task as a starting point. In the image classification  domain, it is very common to use models pre-trained on the  large-scale ImageNet database [17]. Since ImageNet is  orders of magnitude larger than most medical image datasets  it enables training large neural networks without overfitting,  so they learn efficient image feature extraction. This pre- trained model can either be used as a feature extractor, in
which  a new classification model is added and trained on the  output features, or alternatively training is continued with the  same model but on the new task. Transfer learning can  greatly speed up training of new models as well as improve  the model generalizability as it leverages knowledge of  similar tasks previously learned, when compared to training  from scratch [18]. The method of transfer learning used for  this study was “full fine-tuning", which means that none of  the learnable parameters of the pre-trained model were  frozen when training the model for the final task. This  approach was chosen as the optimal number of layers of a  pre-trained model to update is different depending on  network and dataset size and would require individual  adaptation for each tested network [19]. The potential for  overfitting is greater when training the full networks, but this  was compensated for with strong regularization.    2) REGULARIZATION  Current ML models are usually overparameterized meaning  they have a high capacity to overfit the training data. Such a  model can be trained to a point where the model perfectly  learns the samples used in training but does not perform well  on any new data. To avoid overfitting, there are many  different regularization methods applicable to deep learning  that aim to reduce unnecessary complexity in the model [20].  The regularization techniques used in this study were  dropout, batch normalization, stochastic depth, early  stopping, weight decay, label smoothing and data  augmentation.  Histogram equalization  as  a  dataset  preprocessing step was investigated but had a negative effect  on model performance (4.9% mean decrease in accuracy  across the thirteen tested networks compared to the baseline).    3) DATA AUGMENTATION  One of the primary techniques used in DL to avoid  overfitting and improve generalization is data augmentation  [21]. It is achieved by training a model using many copies of  each data sample with different small modifications. For  image classification models it is common to use geometric  transformations, color space adjustments and other image  distortions as augmentations. For this study we used the  automatic augmentation method TrivialAugment [22],  which randomly applies one of many different image  operations at a random strength to each sample. Of the  fourteen total augmentations that are sampled from, eleven  also has a strength, and three are binary choice. The  implementation of TrivialAugment used in the study is from  TorchVision, where details of each augmentation can be  found [23].    4) DEALING WITH NOISY LABELS  The “ground truth” of the TM images in the three public  datasets were all based on the classification of one or a few  otolaryngologists [9], [10], [11]. membrane is challenging, even for experts. In a study by  Sandström et al. five experts individually assessed 347 TM  images and classified them into six diagnoses (dataset D)  [14]. In ten percent of cases a majority decision could not be  reached. Given this difficulty, all the datasets are likely to  include some misclassified images, and the issue is likely  worse when the ground truth is decided by a single person  [24]. In supervised learning this is commonly referred to as  a problem of noisy labels, and it can harm the generalization  performance of a deep learning model. Different  regularization techniques and robust training strategies can  be used to alleviate the issue, but as strong regularization also  tends to decrease model performance, the amount of  incorrectly labelled data should be minimized [25].    5) HYPERPARAMETER OPTIMIZATION  Hyperparameters are the parameters that control the DL  training process but are not part of the final model. When the  amount of training data is limited, it is especially important  to optimize the hyperparameters to get the best performance  for a given neural network [26].
B. DATA SOURCES  1) ETHICS  This study included three public otoscopic image datasets as  well as two that have not been made publicly available. The  collection and sharing of the images in each of these datasets  were done after approval from each of the respective ethical  review boards [9], [10], [11], [14], [15], [16]. The Swedish  Ethical Review Authority has granted ethical approval for  the use of newly collected data in this study and has stated  after review that no additional ethical approval is required  for the use of the existing data material.    2) TYMPANIC MEMBRANE IMAGE DATASETS  The five separate TM image datasets used in this study are  labelled as dataset A, B, C, D and E. Since each dataset  contains a different set of pathologic ear conditions and we  want to evaluate models trained on any of them against any  of the others we divide each dataset into two groups: normal  and abnormal. Images where the TM is not visible were  excluded. The details of each dataset are summarized in  Table 1.  Specifics of how each dataset was collected and how the  ‘ground truth’ labels were determined are available in the  original publications [9], [10], [11], [14], [15], [16]. Datasets  A, B and C were used with class labels as originally  published (labelled ‘original’), or after additional review  including removal and reclassification of some images
(labelled ‘corrected’). The images from datasets C, D and E  did not always have the TM centered in the image so another  preprocessing step was applied to these datasets to center the  TM in the image and crop out any black borders. This step  also mitigates a specific bias identified by Xu et al. [13], who  found that in the Ohio/USA dataset (dataset C) abnormal  cases were frequently framed as partial views while normal  cases captured the entire tympanic membrane, allowing a  model to exploit framing rather than pathology. Centering  and cropping to the tympanic membrane standardizes the  field of view across diagnoses and reduces this confound.  This version of the datasets was labelled ‘centered’. An  advantage of this was that less image detail is lost when  shrinking the image to fit the model input size.   A pooled dataset was made by combining all images from A,  B and C. When using this combined set for training, the  remaining datasets D and E were used as an external test set  (DE n=481). This version was labelled ‘combined’ and  ensured that each image class (ear pathology) in the test set  was also part of the datasets used for training.  Each of the five datasets were randomly divided into train,  validation, and test splits, with 70%, 10%, and 20% of the  images, respectively. ‘Normal’ and ‘abnormal’ classes were  split separately to ensure train/validation/test splits had the  same ratio between the classes. For the combined dataset the  train and validation splits from A, B and C were merged as  training set and the remaining 20% were used as the internal  validation set (ABC train n=1831, ABC validation n=456,  ABC corrected train n=750, ABC corrected validation  n=187). Dataset A contains one image per patient. Dataset B  contains several images per patient, and C has multiple  images of the same ear only for the ‘ventilation tube’ class.  Dataset D and E contain one image per ear per patient.  Patient-level leakage between the training and external test  sets is not possible by design, as datasets A, B and C (used  for training) and datasets D and E (used as the external test  set) are entirely separate collections with no shared subjects.  Within the combined training set, images from the same  patient may appear across the training and validation splits  for dataset B, which contains multiple images per subject ear.  This is an acknowledged limitation; however, since the  validation set is used only for early stopping and not for  model selection across experimental conditions, any within- patient similarity would affect the stopping point rather than  inflate the external generalization estimates. Dataset A and  datasets D and E each contain one image per patient, and  dataset C contains multiple images per ear only for the  ventilation tube class.

IMPROVING TYMPANIC MEMBRANE IMAGE  LABELLING QUALITY  All external images (datasets A, B and C) and their  corresponding diagnoses were systematically reviewed by  two of the authors separately, one senior specialist GP (TL)  and one senior specialist ENT (MW). In a subsequent step,  both reviewers engaged in a consensus discussion, leading to  the exclusion of 506 images due to poor quality, or no  consensus reached. The effect of including poor-quality  images was not evaluated systematically, as images excluded  for quality reasons lacked reliable ground truth labels and  could not be used to assess performance. This is  acknowledged as a limitation; future work could investigate  robustness by simulating quality degradation on retained  images. Additionally, 30 images were reclassified: 29  images initially deemed normal were reclassified as  abnormal, and one image previously marked as abnormal  was reclassified as normal. All reclassifications used the  diagnostic criteria described in Lundberg et al. [15]. The aim  of the re-review was not to guarantee that our revised labels  are more accurate than the originals (given the difficulty of  otoscopic diagnosis, both could contain errors)  but to ensure  that all included images were labelled using a consistent,  documented set of criteria, thereby reducing the inter-rater  component of label noise across datasets.  Dataset B contains multiple images for each subject ear  selected from a video source. For the corrected version only  a single image per ear is kept, which explains the large  number of excluded images.
D. MODEL IMPLEMENTATION DETAILS  1) IMAGE PRE-PROCESSING  Because the datasets have different resolutions and aspect  ratios the images must be resized to match the input size of  the pre-trained neural networks (models). The method used  was to pad rectangular images with black pixels to get equal  height and width, and then resize to 224x224 pixels, which  was the input size used for all models. Pixel values were then  scaled to the range 0 to 1 and normalized by channel-wise  subtraction of the mean and division by the standard  deviation. The mean and standard deviation used was  obtained from ImageNet according to convention. This  transformation was used when evaluating the models. When  training,  there  was  additional  data  augmentation  transformations which were applied after padding the image  to a square.    2) NEURAL NETWORK ARCHITECTURES  Thirteen different artificial neural networks were included in  this study, listed in Table 2. These four architectures were  included to allow direct comparison with the published  baseline of Habib et al. [12]. Nine additional architectures  were included to broaden the comparison across model type  (CNN and Transformer) and size (1.5M–303M parameters);  all thirteen networks are listed in Table 2. VGG, ResNet and  Densenet are common baseline CNN architectures.  MobileNet is included to cover smaller networks, while  EfficientNet is included as a newer architecture with several  optimizations. VisionTransformer was included as it is the  typical baseline Transformer model for image classification.

VisionTransformer  L-16  2020  303.3    3) TRAINING METHODS AND HYPERPARAMETERS  Our training baseline aimed to replicate the results of Habib  et al. [12] using the same method and hyperparameters. The  parameters that were not published were set at defaults or  adjusted to reach the same model accuracy.  We also developed an optimized training approach that uses  recent best practices for training speed, stability, data  efficiency and regularization (Table 3). These parameters  were optimized through a limited grid search choosing the  combination that gave the highest average Matthews  correlation coefficient (MCC) on the same networks and  datasets (A, B, C) as used by Habib et al. to evaluate   generalizability [12]. The neural network optimization  algorithm is AdamW [28] with a learning rate schedule of  “cosine annealing with warm restarts” [29]. Additionally, we  used loss scaling for class imbalance and label smoothing  [30]. Binary cross-entropy (BCE) is the loss function for  both the baseline and optimized methods.  We set maximum training epochs to 200 with a minimum of  30. Early stopping is implemented with a patience period of  20 epochs, meaning that when the evaluation metric has not  improved for 20 epochs the training stops, and the version  with the best performance is kept. This is evaluated on the  internal validation split of the current dataset. The evaluation  metric for the baseline is BCE, meaning the model with the  lowest validation loss is chosen. For the optimized training  method, we instead use MCC as the evaluation metric. MCC  is chosen as both accuracy, F1-score and area under the
receiver  operating  characteristic  (AUROC)  can  be  problematic with imbalanced datasets [31], [32].  We used PyTorch [27] as the framework for model training,  and it was run on a Windows 10 desktop computer with Intel  Core i9-11900K CPU and Nvidia RTX A4000 GPU. The  source code is available at https://github.com/manfred- lindmark/generalizable-image-classification.  4) AUGMENTATION METHODS  Two data augmentation strategies were compared as well as  using no augmentation at all. These variants are labelled ‘no  augment’, ‘classic’ and ‘multi-sample trivial augment’  (MSTA). The classic augmentation consists of random 90°  rotation, random flip (mirroring) and a resize to 256x256  followed by a random crop to 224x224 (effectively X and Y  translation). For every epoch of training new augmented  images were generated.  MSTA is a combination of the ‘wide’ variant of  TrivialAugment  automatic  augmentation  method  as  described by Müller and Hutter 2021 [22], combined with  the technique of drawing multiple augmentation samples per  image [33]. The implementation details and augmentation  parameter  ranges  can  be  found  in  our  code.  Random horizontal flip was included because the model does  not need to know if the image is of a left or right ear, it does  not affect the diagnostic features.  Zoom transformations are present in classic and MSTA  designs: the MSTA method includes random scaling  transforms, and the classic augmentation applies a random  crop after resizing (256→224), which introduces effective  translation and a small zoom.  Batch size during training is 32 when using classic or no  augmentation. With MSTA each batch consists of 8 samples  from the dataset with 12 augmentations per sample for an  effective batch size of 96 at each iteration during training.  This means that for ‘no augment’ and ‘classic’, the number  of training images per epoch was equal to the number of  images in the training dataset (one augmentation per image).  With MSTA each epoch contains 12 times the number of  train images in the dataset, as there are 12 augmentations  made per image at each training step.

E. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN  1) SINGLE DATASET GENERALIZABILITY  Generalizability after training on a single dataset was  evaluated by training models on one of the five and testing  on each of the remaining four. This provides a comparison  of performance between an internal and external test set. The  method corresponds to Habib et al. [12] and we used the  same four networks: ResNet-50, DenseNet-161, VGG16,  VisionTransformer B-16. Each network was trained in four  separate configurations: ‘Baseline’, ‘Corrected data’,  ‘Optimized method’ and ‘Corrected data & optimized  method’. Model training was repeated five times for each  configuration. ‘Baseline’ represents the previously described  baseline hyperparameters with no augmentation and the  original datasets. ‘Corrected data’ is the baseline training
method but with the corrected and centered versions of each  dataset. ‘Optimized method’ is the original datasets but with  optimized hyperparameters and MSTA augmentation.  Finally, the last configuration uses both corrected data and  the optimized training method. A schematic view of this  experiment can be seen in Figure 2.   2) NEURAL NETWORK ARCHITECTURE COMPARISON  The differences between all thirteen networks were  investigated by training each on the combined dataset. The  same four configurations were used (baseline, corrected data,  optimized method, corrected data & optimized method) and  training was repeated five times for each network and  configuration (see ‘Network comparison’ in Figure 2).
FIGURE 2. Schematic view of the three experiments. Each row of each box in Data is one version of a dataset used to train each of the networks, and  separately with each method in the Methods boxes. Single dataset training: 5 + 3 datasets × 4 networks × 2 training methods = 64 combinations.  Network comparison: 2 datasets × 13 networks × 2 training methods = 52 combinations. Generalizability factors: 3 datasets × 2 networks × 2 training  methods × 3 augmentation methods = 36 combinations. Each combination in each experiment is run with 5 repeats, giving a total of 320, 260, and 180  trained models for the experiments respectively. Each of the  36 experimental configurations was replicated five times  with five different random seeds (set as 1-5, repeated for  each configuration) to account for stochasticity in neural  network training.  To verify that seeds had no significant effect, we first fit a  linear mixed model with seed as a random intercept. The
intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC=0.0) indicated that  close to 0% of residual variance was attributable to seed  differences, and a likelihood ratio test was not significant  (p=1.00). We therefore proceeded with OLS, treating  observations as independent. This choice was made because  the absence of a meaningful random effect removes the  primary motivation for mixed-effects modelling; OLS is  simpler to interpret and its assumptions are more readily  verifiable.  We compared three models: main effects only, all two-way  interactions, and a parsimonious model that only included  interactions that were significant (α=0.01) in the model with  all interactions. Holm-Bonferroni correction was used to  correct for multiple comparisons. Levene's tests indicated  unequal variances for some factors, so we report  heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (HC3) for all  inferential statistics. Effect sizes are reported as ω2.

DISCUSSION  We highlight the issue of generalizability of image  classification models for middle ear disease classification by  demonstrating that general methods that are easily applied  will improve generalizability in a data-limited setting. We  have shown that the choice of network architecture is less  important than having high data quality and optimizing the  training method.  Previous research has shown the potential for using artificial  intelligence to diagnose ear diseases using otoscopic images  [2], but the standard methods for training a DL image  classifier often lead to a model that generalizes poorly to  images from other sources than its training data [12].  Reproducing and comparing published methods is also  difficult when they require implementing complex neural  network architectures or data processing methods [3]. For  this reason, we have developed methods that improve  generalizability  independently  of  which  network  architecture or dataset that is used and implemented them in  the most commonly used deep learning framework.  The clinical significance of the improvements can be placed  in context against human diagnostic accuracy. Moberly et al.
[23] reported neurotologists as 72% accurate in correctly  identifying an eardrum as normal. Our best model reached  83% accuracy on the external test set (sensitivity 71%,  specificity 91%) for binary classification. While direct  comparison is limited by differences in task definition, this  suggests the optimized model approaches the range of  experienced clinicians for this binary screening task,  particularly relevant in low-resource settings, where  screening already provides value. The sensitivity/specificity  trade-off can be tuned by simply moving the threshold of the  binary classification.  The drop in predictive accuracy when a model trained on a  single dataset is evaluated on another was apparent in our  results (Figure 3). Although the major difference was in part  caused by each dataset including different types of middle  ear diseases, we could also see that an improved method will  bring external test MCC closer to the internal. Another point  to note from the internal/external comparison is that all  methods may look equally effective when only looking at  internal MCC (Figure 3). This suggests that comparing or  selecting the best method using only an internal performance

metric is not feasible when training, validation, and test data  are from the same collection.  Several distinct sources of domain shift are present. Imaging  hardware differs across datasets, as do patient demographics,  disease prevalence, and age distributions across the  contributing countries, introducing concept shift related to  local epidemiology. The original labelling processes also  differed in the number and specialty of annotators, adding  inter-rater variability as a source of label noise. These factors  explain why the internal-external performance gap is large  even after optimization. Reducing the gap in practice would  require  greater  control  over  acquisition  protocol,  standardized  pre-processing  (resolution,  color  normalization, and centering of the membrane), and ground  truth labelling by multiple annotators with additional  diagnostic features.  From the results of the comparison between different  network architectures (Figure 4) we saw that differences  between architectures were smaller with an optimized  training method, and that network sizes above 20 million  parameters provided no noticeable improvement on this task.  A key takeaway is that training method (hyperparameters,  augmentation) and data quality is much more important than  network architecture choice when starting from a pre-trained  image classification model and training a classifier for TM  images (Figure 4, Figure 6).  The interactions that are visible by looking at Figure 6 show  that all factors have an effect, and generally you get most of  the benefit from optimizing just two or three of them.  Optimizing all factors resulted in the best classification  model, although the benefits of each factor overlap in parts.  The OLS model shows that the biggest positive coefficients  were optimized regularization (training method) and MSTA  augmentation. The interaction of these two has a negative  coefficient, which suggests that they in some respect solve  the same generalization problem. The same thing was seen  in the interaction between the better network architecture and  the optimized regularization. There are positive but smaller  effects from network and data pre-processing.  Another observation was that the corrected data had a  positive effect especially with the classic augmentation  method. This, and the fact that classic augmentation was  worse than no augmentation with the uncorrected data  suggests that the classic augmentation does not prevent  overfitting to the training images, and if the dataset also  includes more mis-labelled cases, this even decreases  performance by helping the model learn incorrect labels.  We note that since interaction terms were selected based on  significance with the given data, the p-values of these could  be optimistically biased. The model’s main purpose is  exploratory, to make it easier to identify the largest  interaction effects.  None of the applied methods are exclusive to otoscopic  image classifiers but could be applied to any medical image  classification  task  using  deep learning. The only
consideration would be adapting the set of augmentations,  since certain image transformations like color distortions or  rotation would not be suitable in all domains.   The binary (normal/abnormal) framing was a deliberate  design choice. The five datasets do not share a consistent set  of pathological classes, and no single class is represented  across all five; a multiclass evaluation would therefore  require restricting the analysis to a subset of classes or  datasets, which would greatly reduce the benefit of having  all five unique sources. A binary classifier is also clinically  meaningful as a first-stage screening tool. Further challenges  will arise in the multiclass setting, including severe class  imbalance and the difficult distinction of OME. These are  important directions for future work, and the generalization- improving methods demonstrated here are expected to  remain applicable at the multiclass level, since the  underlying domain shift mechanisms are independent of the  number of classes. The diagnoses that are difficult to assess  visually might require other modalities of data to diagnose  with certainty. Since we have seen a quality issue of the  ground truth labels from several data sources, for future data  collection it is preferable to have more than one expert’s  opinion on the correct classification, or other diagnostic  assessments that confirm the correct diagnosis. A recent  literature review by Rony et al. [34] focusing on AI driven  advancements in otitis diagnosis notes that a key weakness  of current research is the lack of involvement of medical  experts in both developing and validating the diagnostic AI  models. Clear distinctions in how to set the ground truth in  training data are necessary to avoid the inter-rater variability  source of domain shift.  A limitation in this study was that hyperparameters were not  optimized for each model and augmentation method  individually,  for  example  by  using  automatic  hyperparameter tuning. The large number of investigated  models and factors motivated the choice of finding a single  set of optimized hyperparameters that worked well  regardless of other changes. Another limitation was that the  differences between the five datasets may be greater than  what is realistic when implementing a clinical diagnostic  tool, where you would have greater control over image  acquisition, processing and ground truth labelling. The  sources of domain shift between the datasets are several and  compounding: differences in otoscope hardware, in patient  demographics and local disease prevalence across the  contributing countries, and in the original annotation  protocols. Consistent with the recommendations of Xu et al.  [13], reducing this shift in practice would likely require  standardized image acquisition (consistent field of view,  illumination, and centering of the tympanic membrane) and  multi-annotator  ground  truth  labelling.  Additional  limitations include the potential within-patient overlap in the  training/validation split for dataset B (Section II-B); the  binary framing, which does not capture differential diagnosis  between specific conditions; and the limited geographic and

There are some aspects to consider for future work in  improving  the  generalizability  of  medical  image  classification models. When data are limited, as in the case  with TM images, it could be beneficial to pre-train a model  on medical domain images rather than only ImageNet [35].  If a model is trained on other diagnostic tasks involving  healthy versus pathologic images of skin or tissue it is  possible that some of that knowledge would transfer to  recognizing similar features in the ear canal. Another  potential is exploiting the recent advances in foundation  models. Starting from a model with broad capabilities, we  can fine-tune them with smaller amounts of specific data  from our target domain, allowing them to adapt while  preserving their robust general representations. This  adaptability, combined with ongoing advancements in self- supervised and few-shot learning, can make them well-suited  to manage the domain shift we observed in this field and thus  helping maintain accuracy and reliability.    V. CONCLUSION  DL-based image classification models for detecting middle  ear diseases do not generalize well when only trained on a  single source of images, and how much different methods  improve generalizability cannot be evaluated unless they are  tested on a separate external data source with a domain shift.  With a better choice of model training parameters and data  augmentation, models generalize much better when faced  with a domain shift. The presented methods are effective  even without tuning specifically for a certain neural network  or dataset and are easy to implement. The advantage of  improved generalizability is that a model implemented in a  clinical decision support system would not be limited to a  narrow range of otoscopes or patient demographics.

THORBJÖRN LUNDBERG was born in Umeå,  Sweden, in 1965. He received his medical degree  (MD) in 1999, became a specialist in general  practice in 2006 in Umeå, and earned a Ph.D. in  family medicine at Umeå University in 2014.
Since 2019, he has held a position as Senior  Lecturer in Public Health and Clinical Medicine,  Family Medicine, at Umeå University, and works  as  a  General  Practitioner  within  Region  Västerbotten. He is the author of 11 scientific  articles. His research interests include the diagnosis of ear disease and the  development of new technologies to improve diagnostic accuracy. He is the principal investigator of the eHEar project, which focuses on  innovative applications to improve and facilitate access to diagnostics for  otitis media and hearing impairment. He has also served as an expert in  developing treatment guidelines for otitis media and rhinosinusitis in 2010,  2019, and 2025 in collaboration with the Swedish Medical Products  Agency.
MIMMI WERNER was born in Sweden in 1968.  She  graduated  from  Karolinska  Institutet,  Stockholm, Sweden, in 1994 as Medical Doctor.  She has been a specialized otorhinolaryngologist  since 2008. PhD, MD Werner is an elected member of the Swedish Society of  Otosurgery, and the Swedish ACTA Oto-Laryngologica Society.
PAOLO SODA (Member, IEEE) received the  graduation degree with honours in biomedical  engineering from University Campus Bio- Medico (UCBM), Rome, in 2004, and the PhD  degree in biomedical engineering (computer  science area) from University Campus Bio- Medico (UCBM), Rome, in 2008.

FREDRIK ÖHBERG was born in Umeå, Sweden,  in 1969. He received the M.S. degree in physics,  with a focus on computational physics and  measurement technology, from Umeå University,  Umeå, Sweden, in 1993, and the Ph.D. degree in  biomedical engineering from the Department of  Radiation Sciences, Umeå University, in 2009. We therefore proceeded with OLS, treating  observations as independent. This choice was made because  the absence of a meaningful random effect removes the  primary motivation for mixed-effects modelling; OLS is  simpler to interpret and its assumptions are more readily  verifiable.  We compared three models: main effects only, all two-way  interactions, and a parsimonious model that only included  interactions that were significant (α=0.01) in the model with  all interactions. Holm-Bonferroni correction was used to  correct for multiple comparisons. Levene's tests indicated  unequal variances for some factors, so we report  heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors (HC3) for all  inferential statistics. Effect sizes are reported as ω2.

STATISTICAL ANALYSIS  When comparing the OLS models with main effects, selected  interactions  (parsimonious  model),  or  all  two-way  interactions a few observations can be made. R2 increased  substantially by including interactions, from 0.70 to 0.82  with significant interactions, and 0.83 with all interactions.  Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) values were  respectively −444, −500 and −482, motivating the choice of

the parsimonious model. Full models, ANOVA, effect sizes,  simple effects and assumption checks are available in the  supplementary materials.  Figure 6 shows all observations split into four plots to show  the interactions of different factors. Three interactions had  large effect sizes (ω2>0.14) when looking at the simple  effects. They are preprocessing effect with ‘classic  augmentation’,  augmentation  method  with  ‘baseline  regularization’, and finally regularization method with ‘no  augmentation’.
